utterances.text: This document entitled "Occupancy Certificate" or, rather, "Property Certificate," was issued in 1999, and it emanates from it that among others, the owner is Stipo Alilovic, son of Pero. So in 1999, reference is made to an owner of whom we know, without any doubt, that he died in 1995. So it's a document that is outdated and doesn't point to the proper conclusions. In other words, the owner is a person who died several years previously, so the document is not reliable, in our view. Of course, it is up to you to assess it. I don't know what purpose it can serve.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: A very short observation, if I'm allowed. I had indeed served these documents to the Defence. They show that Stipo Alilovic and the witness were owners of real estate property in Santici and in the area, in that area of Central Bosnia. This was not challenged by the witness. Therefore, I believe that these documents are not that useful, and of course I shall defer to the Tribunal's decision. They were created on the 20th of April, 1992, and they mentioned property owned by Stipo Alilovic. That doesn't seem much of a problem to me, inasmuch as mention was not made of his death, and the mention relating to the legacy settlement was not communicated to the relevant services in Bosnia. I only attach relative pertinence or relevance to this document because the witness did not challenge that the property was, well, the family's property, and that was the thing that mattered to me. Let us mention another document, the one drafted by the HVO on the 12th of February, 1993, in Travnik. I do not claim that the document was drafted by the Vitez HVO. I presented the document as a document being made in Travnik, and I asked the witness whether this rang a bell in the witness's mind. I do not claim anything else, as far as this document is concerned. I submitted it to the witness. The document was drafted in compliance with the then legislation in the Bosnian Croatian community, and as such, it does have some relevance. If that came to be necessary, we would have to prove that a similar document had been drafted for the Vitez municipality or that this document, related to Travnik, also applied to Vitez. The document is what it is at face value. I do not claim that it is anything else. It was established by the Travnik municipality, it was submitted to the witness, and the witness said that she had never heard of it. That's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I may be allowed another brief comment. In the first place, I have to say to the Prosecutor that the documents he's referring to, and I am referring to the property documents, do not talk about property, as he says. They talk about ownership. At least those of us belonging to the area know the distinction. As for the other document, I have already said why I felt that it was not relevant as an exhibit in this case, because to see whether there is any unified legislation for the whole area of Bosnia, that is another matter. We're talking about Vitez. That is all I would have to say. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Counsel Slokovic-Glumac?

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Mr. President, just one sentence linked to this document which was apparently issued by the Travnik HVO. I would like to note that the witness did not recognise that document at all. She didn't recognise it in contents, nor the author, nor the signature. Therefore, she knows nothing about that document. On these grounds, I feel that it cannot be admitted into evidence, and still less can any analogy be made, mentioned by the Prosecutor, that there may have been a similar document in Vitez municipality. Therefore, we really do feel that this document cannot be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Before ruling on this matter, may I ask two questions of Defence counsel? First of all, you made a distinction between ownership and property. Could you clarify this matter? Secondly, could you clarify why, in the certificates of occupancy, mention is made of Cadastral county, Travnik, and then Cadastral municipality, Ahmici? What is the relation between Ahmici and Travnik? Does Ahmici belong to Travnik? Does it come within the purview of Travnik, from the viewpoint of Cadastral matters? Two questions, therefore.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: First, your question of ownership. This document, issued by the Cadastral office and a document that would prove ownership, would have been issued by the competent court or its land registrar where data are kept on ownership and on property, similarly on all the liabilities stemming from that property. So the competent court issues a document on ownership or, rather, its department for land registry, where the books are kept, and they issue the certificates. These lands ownership books are public documents, and everyone is free to access them. At the same time, owners may be possessors and they may not be possessors or owners, especially if the situation is not regular, because someone may sell or give away his property as a gift without that procedure being registered in the appropriate documents, so that in the land registrars you will find the name of one person as the owner, and the use of that property may be held by another person. That, unfortunately, is the reality in the areas in which we live, and not only there. As for this document -- oh, there was another question, I'm sorry, the question of the municipality and the municipal court in Vitez. They have the land registers where the property is registered for the municipality of Vitez, and there is a Cadastral department there and, in this connection, also fiscal bodies, and this has nothing to do with property registered somewhere else because that property is registered over there. If I am looking for data about my property, I have to address all those bodies or, rather, courts on whose territory that property is situated. Then I will receive full, complete data about my total property. I'm referring to immovable property, land, forests, houses. To sum up, this document just shows that Stipo Alilovic as well as this witness, in those days, I suppose, and are still now registered as the owners of this immovable property. Whether they actually had the right of use of that property is another matter. We have to look through the land registers in the competent courts to see this. If any decision were to be taken on confiscation or seizure, it would have to be based on seizing something from somebody that was the actual owner, and we would have to verify whether they were the real owners. I'm not sure that I have been very clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. (Trial Chamber deliberates)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes. In light of the various explanations given, we have decided to admit these documents into evidence. It will, of course, be for the Court to decide upon the probative value, if any, of these documents. So they are admitted into evidence. Again I would like to thank the witness for her patience, and she may now be released.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, but we have not decided yet whether we shall keep the original documents or shall we make a copy of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: A copy, because the witness has, of course, the right to keep the original for obvious psychological reasons. Photocopies, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's what I thought. Thank you. (The witness withdrew)

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The Post Bank ID will be C10, and Mrs. Krizanac's passport will be C11.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Your Honour, for things to be clear, in Prosecutor's Exhibit 358, you have got the four certificates of occupancy and also the HVO decision regarding the Travnik municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: The witness, I think it's Mr. Simovic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "Did you mention the passport," says the Presiding Judge, turning to the Court Deputy.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The passport of who?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: No, the passport of the husband -- no, for Marie. All right. So shall we bring in Mr. Simovic? (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Simovic. I would like to ask you to make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you so much. You may sit down. Counsel Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Examined by Mr. Krajina:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Simovic.

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SIMOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you please tell us your name first and your last name, the year of your birth, and what is your place of residence?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SIMOVIC
utterances.text: My name is Radoslav Simovic, born on the 29th of November, 1931, born in Citluk, a place in Herzegovina, and I live now in Baska Voda, near Makarska. It is about 50 kilometres from Split, to the east.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. What are you?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SIMOVIC
utterances.text: I own a restaurant/pub. I mean tourism, anything to do with catering, restaurant, hostelry business.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You told us you live in Baska Voda. Where is Baska Voda, what state?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SIMOVIC
utterances.text: It is in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see, in Croatia. How far is Baska Voda from Vitez?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SIMOVIC
utterances.text: It is some 200 kilometres from Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And from Split?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SIMOVIC
utterances.text: From Split, it is 50 kilometres away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I shall slow down, and I shall also ask you to slow down for the sake of the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yeah, I see. All right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you please tell us -- you told us you were in the hostelry business. Do you have a house, a flat? What do you have?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SIMOVIC
utterances.text: I have a house. I have a house in Baska Voda; 15 rooms, 40 beds. There are three beds to a room. It is about a hundred metres from the coast.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. When did you go to live in Baska Voda?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SIMOVIC
utterances.text: I went there before the war. It must have been sometime in '87 or thereabouts when I went to live there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Where did you live before that?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SIMOVIC
utterances.text: Before that, I again had a coffee pub at the mouth of the Lasva River into the Bosna River.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. Thank you. Do you know Vlatko Kupreskic?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SIMOVIC
utterances.text: I know Vlatko Kupreskic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How well do you know him?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SIMOVIC
utterances.text: I know him very well indeed. I know both him and his family, his relative, Ivica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since when have you known Vlatko?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SIMOVIC
utterances.text: Over ten years, must be. I wouldn't know exactly, but it must be over ten years. I reckon that is how long I've known him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. During all the time that you knew him, on what kind of terms were you? Were you acquaintances or good friends or what?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SIMOVIC
utterances.text: Well, we were on very good, friendly terms, particularly with his relative, with his cousin Ivica, with whom we had two outlets on two sides of Zenica. That is where we worked, and we knew one another and visited one another and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. You said "Ivica." What is his surname?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SIMOVIC
utterances.text: Kupreskic, Ivica Kupreskic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Could you tell us if, in 1993 and otherwise before the war, on the eve of the war, if Vlatko came to Croatia, did he drop by to see you or so?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I used to see him when Ivica and Ivica's wife and he came, and Ivica's wife came from some foreign country, I believe it was from Germany, and that is when they came.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They came to your place?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they came to me, and it was as the sun was setting in Baska Voda.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why did they come?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SIMOVIC
utterances.text: Well, they came to spend the night there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did they?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they did spend the night there, and they left early in the morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Will you tell us, do you remember how they came and where did they come from?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SIMOVIC
utterances.text: They came from Split.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From Split. Did they tell you what business they had in Split? Why did they go to Split?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SIMOVIC
utterances.text: Well, they went to meet that woman, Ivica's wife. They went to meet her, and that was already late in the night, and so they came to my place and they spent the night there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Will you tell us -- we have to wait for the interpretation. Do you remember, what means of transport did they use?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SIMOVIC
utterances.text: They had a Yugo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is it, a car?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's a car.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Do you remember when it was exactly?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SIMOVIC
utterances.text: It was in the evening of the 14th. On the 15th in the morning, they left, and the war in Bosnia ensued right away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good. Tell us then, you told us they arrived on the 14th?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, in the evening.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And spent the night?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SIMOVIC
utterances.text: And spent the night.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did they leave?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SIMOVIC
utterances.text: They left around 6.00 or 7.00 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did all three of them leave?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, all three of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: By that car?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, by that car.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us also how is it that it stuck in your memory it was the night between the 14th and the 15th?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SIMOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I remembered. I really wanted to know. I had a son who worked in Zenica at the fire brigade, and there was also another one held the coffee pub that I used to run once and he was running now, and therefore I wanted to know what was going on with them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us that the next day, the war broke out?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the war broke out. The roads were closed down, and there was no way --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how did you find out?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SIMOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I saw it all in the media. Television and radio and all this had them on, and that was that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is why you remember that date?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is why I remember that date very well indeed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Will you tell us also if you saw Vlatko after that?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did see him after that on various occasions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many times, when was that?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SIMOVIC
utterances.text: Well, a few years after the war. I don't remember exactly, but he came to see me, as I did see him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Tell me, when they spent that evening with you, do you remember what the conversation was about?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SIMOVIC
utterances.text: Well, we had a normal conversation, a friendly one. We had our dinner, had a drink or two, and in the morning my wife saw them off to Bosnia, to Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: I see. Right. Thank you. Thank you very much, Mr. Simovic. I have no further questions, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you for being so concise, and we can now take a 15-minute break.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: I shall try and be as brief as Mr. Krajina was. Could you tell us, before the war or since the war, did you have any professional relationship with the accused Vlatko Kupreskic or with his family?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SIMOVIC
utterances.text: No, I just knew them. That was all.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Witness, as of 1987, you ran a hotel in Baska Voda, and you said that you had some 15 rooms in that hotel; is that so?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SIMOVIC
utterances.text: (No translation)

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: What were the patrons, the customers, in late '92, early '93? What kind of people would come and put up at your hotel?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SIMOVIC
utterances.text: Well, anyone could come to my hotel. The peak season was from the 1st of June until the 30th of September. After that, it would be cold; winter would come.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: As a hotel owner, didn't you have to keep a book in which you mentioned everybody staying for the night in your hotel?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but earlier on, I used to work with companies, with firms. I would rent them rooms, and they would keep track of the names of the guests and how long they stayed, for their employees.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, my question was as follows: You, as a hotel owner, you had, didn't you, you had the obligation, for the police or revenue purposes, you had to keep a register, a book, in which you mentioned the names of every guest? Wasn't that one of your obligations?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SIMOVIC
utterances.text: Off season.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Could you be more specific? Did you have such obligations during the season, or off season, or what was the situation?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SIMOVIC
utterances.text: Off season.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: In other words, you are telling us that when it wasn't high season or shoulder, you didn't have to keep a book, a log, whilst you had such obligations when it was the season?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Therefore, you mentioned the fact that Vlatko Kupreskic, Ivica Kupreskic, and Vlatko's wife were at the hotel nowhere, in no document whatsoever?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SIMOVIC
utterances.text: I have no written document, because other people who would stay as friends would never fill in any forms.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Do you remember if Vlatko Kupreskic was put up only once, or several times, in your hotel?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SIMOVIC
utterances.text: Several times.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: So he visited you several times, did he?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SIMOVIC
utterances.text: (No interpretation)

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Could you tell us more specifically when he came, and whether he was always together with Ivica Kupreskic, and how frequent their visits were?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SIMOVIC
utterances.text: They usually occurred in the off-season months. They would travel on business, and how do I know what are the reasons he had to travel? And he would drop by.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Let us mention the first months of 1993. Do you remember whether Vlatko Kupreskic visited you on several occasions in those first months of 1993, and if there were such visits, how frequent they were?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SIMOVIC
utterances.text: No, just the last time he came, on the 14th, when the war was on in Bosnia, he visited me, and he spent the night with Ivica and Ivica's wife as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: So he was there on the 14th of April; when else did he visit you?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SIMOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot remember him coming at all in that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Witness, I'd like us to understand each other properly. You said just a moment ago that Vlatko Kupreskic visited you several times. When, exactly, did he visit you? Could you be more specific? If you can't remember, well, let us know, equally.

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SIMOVIC
utterances.text: He always came in the off-season months, that is, during the winter and the like.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Here is my ensuing question: In the winter following April 1993, did Vlatko Kupreskic visit you? Did he do so on several occasions? How frequent were the visits? Was he together with Ivica Kupreskic, or would he travel alone?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SIMOVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember at all. All I remember is this one time that he came, and that was on the 14th and the 15th, when Ivica and his wife were with him. I can't remember whether he came again in the course of that year or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: So let's make things clear, because I have the feeling that your answers to my question are somewhat vague. You perfectly remember Vlatko's, Ivica's, and Ivica's wife's visit on the 14th of April, 1993. You remember that visit perfectly well. However, you have no memory whatsoever of other visits they may have made to you?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SIMOVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember any other visit. I didn't take note of it, nor did I record it anywhere, because I have an apartment there, I have my family, and they would come to visit, but not during the season. During the season, a record is kept of people who come.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Do you know that Vlatko Kupreskic would go rather frequently to Croatia?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SIMOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I can't remember. I don't know that he came often. He may have gone somewhere else, but he didn't come to see me. How could I know?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Would you know where he might have gone if he wasn't going to visit you?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SIMOVIC
utterances.text: I couldn't know. I couldn't say. I don't know who else he had.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Witness, since you have only very dim memories of the period before April '93, since you kept no written trace or track of your visitors in the off-season period, how can you be so sure when it comes to the date of the 14th or 15th of April 1993?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SIMOVIC
utterances.text: I can remember because there was a war in Bosnia, and it was not possible to travel. I had two sons in Bosnia, one in Zenica, one in Lasva, some 15 kilometres away, where there was a coffee bar, and I was interested because of my children more than anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Do you remember whether Ivica Kupreskic mentioned to you the state of war that was prevailing in Central Bosnia at the time? Well, it might have been Ivica or Vlatko Kupreskic.

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SIMOVIC
utterances.text: I can't remember them telling me anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: You told us that they travelled in a Yugo 45 car?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Was there anything striking or unusual about that car that you would have noticed?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SIMOVIC
utterances.text: I really can't remember. It was an ordinary car.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Did you notice whether it was a fully-loaded or heavily-loaded car?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SIMOVIC
utterances.text: I couldn't remember that. My apartment is on the fourth floor of the building, and I didn't even go down. They came upstairs, they parked the car in the garage, and that's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Did they use a telephone from your hotel? Did they phone to Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SIMOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether I had a telephone in the house at the time. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Do you remember whether you had a chat with them?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we talked normally, just like any other people.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Would you remember what you talked about?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SIMOVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember. Just like one would talk to people one knew, we sat together, had dinner, talked about everything. Nothing in particular, nothing specific. We just chatted like comrades.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: You said earlier on, but could you say it again, because I'm not sure I understood very well: You told us that you then had a son, and that he ran a restaurant in Zenica; is that so?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Close to Zenica, on the road outside Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: You also stated that you kept in touch with your son in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SIMOVIC
utterances.text: No. I couldn't when the war started. Before that, I was in touch with him, of course, because I helped him to run the facility.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: This will be my last question, witness. So given the dates when Vlatko, Ivica Kupreskic were put up at your hotel, had the war already started then or not?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SIMOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: As far as you can remember, when after that date did the war start?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SIMOVIC
utterances.text: That same day, the next day, officially.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: And how did you hear of this?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SIMOVIC
utterances.text: I learned it from the television reports. Ivica wouldn't have brought his wife from another country if he knew that there was a war. He brought her as if it were normal, as if there was no war. How do I know what happened afterwards?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Re-examined by Mr. Krajina:

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Let us just clarify one point. My learned friend, the Prosecutor, used on several occasions the word "hotel" as if it was a real hotel -- just a moment, please, just a moment. Hear me out. The Prosecutor spoke about a hotel. My question is, do you own a hotel -- you know what a hotel is -- or do you own a house in which you rent rooms for tourists?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SIMOVIC
utterances.text: A house.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Is that a hotel?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SIMOVIC
utterances.text: No. It's not a hotel, but it is quite big. There are 15 rooms.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Does it say "Hotel" on it?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SIMOVIC
utterances.text: No. It's considered private accommodation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. We have no questions. Mr. Simovic, thank you so much for coming. I assume there is no objection to the witness being released, so therefore the witness may now be released. Thank you. (The witness withdrew)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: We may move on to our next witness. (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mrs. Kupreskic. Will you please make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated. Counsel Par?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Par:

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mrs. Kupreskic.

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Will you first of all introduce yourself, tell the Court your name, when and where you were born, and your occupation.

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: My name is Ljubica Kupreskic. I am the wife of the unfairly accused Vlatko Kupreskic. I was born on the 5th of April, 1962, in a place called Jardol, Vitez municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: How long have you been married to Vlatko?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: With the innocently accused Vlatko Kupreskic, I have been since 1982.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Will you please not repeat this phrase, "innocently accused." Just answer the questions directly. How many children do you have?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: We have two children, a 16-year-old daughter and a son of 12.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Could you tell us how long you have been living in Pirici?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: I have been living in Pirici since I joined the Kupreskic family, that is, in 1982, and I am still living there to this day.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Could you tell us who owns this house? Is it Vlatko's house or his father's house?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Both the old and the new house is in Vlatko's father's name, because when we built the new house, all of us together moved into the new house, from the old house into the new house.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: On the 16th of April, 1993, who was living in that house?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Vlatko's parents, I, Vlatko, and our two children.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: So you lived in an enlarged family with Vlatko's parents, or did you have two separate households?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: We lived together with Vlatko's parents. It was a single household.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Would you please give us the names of your nearest neighbours, first the Croats and then the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: My nearest neighbours, Croats, are Mirko Vidovic, Gordana and Milko Vidovic, Stipan Vidovic, Ivica Kupreskic, Zoran Kupreskic, Anto Kupreskic, Mirjan Kupreskic, Ivo Kupreskic. My nearest Muslim neighbours are Sakib Ahmic, Sukrija Ahmic, Ramiz Gradinovic, Sabahudin Muratovic, Ismail Pezer, Sulejman Pezer.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: I should now like us to focus on the period from 1992 until the conflict of the 16th of April '93. So could you please tell us, in that period, '92/93, what was Vlatko doing?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: In the period from '92 to '93, Vlatko was in trade. He worked in the private company Sutre, together with his cousin, Ivica Kupreskic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: In that period, did Vlatko engage in any political activities? What I mean is, did he become a member of any political party? Was he politically active? Did he speak in public or was he politically committed in any way?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Vlatko never -- was never politically active. He was never a member of any party.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: In that same period, '92/93, did anything change in terms of his attitude towards the Muslims who were your neighbours and customers?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Vlatko's attitude never changed in relation to anyone, either the Muslims or the Serbs, his customers or his neighbours. His attitude was always the same. It was a correct attitude. He never distinguished people by their nationality but by their qualities, whether they were good or bad people.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Tell us, was Vlatko mobilised in that period?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: No, he was not mobilised.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Was there any reason for that? Had he served in the army?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Vlatko did not serve in the former Yugoslavia army because he is a heart patient. He is 100 per cent disabled, and for that, he was released from the duty of serving in the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Talking about this disease, do you know what kind of ailment he has? And my additional question would be: Could you tell us how this disease manifests itself in everyday life?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: The heart trouble that Vlatko has is manifested in such a way that he gets tired quickly, that his palms perspire. He is not resilient to physical effort.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Do you know the diagnosis?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: I don't know, but I know the symptoms because I've been living with him, and I know them very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know whether Vlatko in those days, '92/93, participated in the village guards?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: No, Vlatko never participated in village guards.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: In that period, did Vlatko have any kind of weapon?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: No, Vlatko did not have a weapon in that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: I should now like to ask you, for us, to focus on the 14th, 15th, and 16th of March 1993, that is, prior to the conflict in Ahmici. Do you recall what Vlatko was doing on the 14th and 15th of April 1993, that is, two days prior to the conflict in Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Could you tell us, please, in brief?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Yes. On the 14th of April, 1993, Vlatko went on a business trip together with Ivica Kupreskic to Split.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: In view of the fact that we have had occasion to hear quite a bit about this trip, I will only ask you a couple of questions specifically related to that business trip. Do you know when Vlatko left on this trip?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do know exactly. He left on the 14th of April, early in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Didn't he leave on the 13th? Could it be the 13th, because Vlatko said so on one occasion? Will you please think about that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: He did not leave on the 13th, because on the official order, there is the date of the 13th, and it was usually the date on the eve of anybody's business trip. That was the order for the business trip that was issued by the municipality. It was always the previous date to the date of the travel.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: How can you be so sure it was the 14th?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: I can be sure because I know that Ivica Kupreskic's wife was coming back from Germany and that the plane was to land down in Split around 1.00, and that is how I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: We are still on that business trip. With whom did Vlatko go off, and what means of transportation did he take?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Vlatko set off with Ivica Kupreskic, who was the manager of the Sutre company, and they took the car, the Yugo 45.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Could you tell us, when did he come back?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: He returned from the business trip on the 15th of April, '93, around 7.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: And who came back with him?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Ivica Kupreskic and his wife, Ankica Kupreskic, came back with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Do you know if Vlatko brought some merchandise with him?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I know that he did bring some merchandise with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Could you tell us what?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: It was fabrics or, rather, clothes. There were jeans, children's jeans, and underwear.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Do you know what one was supposed to do with that merchandise?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do know what one was supposed to do with that merchandise. Part of this had been ordered for Travnik for Mr. Nevzudin Filipovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Will you please tell us, how is it that you know that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Vlatko told me that Nevzudin had ordered some merchandise from him.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Will you tell us who Nevzudin Filipovic is?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Nevzudin Filipovic married Vlatko's sister, so he is our brother-in-law.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Did they have a shop or what?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Yes, they had a shop in Travnik. It was called Private Company Lasva.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Right. We're finished with this business trip now. Will you please tell us, what did you personally do that day, the 15th of April, the day before the conflict at Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: On the 15th of April, '93, I was taking my driving test with the automotive society in Vitez, and it was at 16.00, that is, at 4.00 in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: You're saying that you took your driving test?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: So when you came back from the test, when was it?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: I came home around 6.00 in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: On the 15th of April?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: On the 15th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Then did you, around your house or around the shop, did you see anything out of the ordinary? Did you see any soldiers? Did perhaps some soldiers come or something that was out of the ordinary? Did you see anything?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: I did not see anything out of the ordinary. It was like any other day. I know that that day my daughter went to school there in Ahmici. All the children were at school. There was nothing unusual. It was like all the previous days.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Did any member of your family tell you perhaps that that day soldiers appeared in the house or in the shop?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: No, nobody told me. If anything like that had happened, they would have presumably told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: The night between the 15th and the 16th of April, was that a quiet night? Rather, my question is how did you pass that night at home and who was at home that night?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Well, that night was quiet, like any other night, and we were there. So Vlatko's parents, Vlatko, myself and our children were in the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Some witnesses testified that that night, the lights were switched on at your house during the night. Could you tell us something about that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: I don't know that anybody switched on the lights that night. Children may have got up.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: But was there any reason? Did somebody move around, switching on the lights?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Well, I myself did not get up and did not switch on the lights. I know nothing about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Right. We've now moved on to the 16th of April, '93. Mrs. Kupreskic, could you tell us what woke you up on the 16th of April, '93?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: On the 16th of April, '93, I was woken up by a telephone call.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Will you please tell us, as of that telephone call, what happened then?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Well, the telephone rang, and I got up and answered. It was a male voice which told me to go to the shelter. But I did not take it seriously, I thought it was a provocation, and then I went back to bed.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Right. We could not hear what the counsel said to the witness.

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: So the telephone rang again, and a male voice once again saying, "What are you waiting for? Why don't you go to the shelter?" I asked, "Who is it," but he would not introduce himself. Then I called Vlatko. Vlatko answered the phone, but then he also went back to bed together with me, and he said, "Oh, forget it. It's a provocation." Then less than 15 minutes or so later, the telephone rang once again, and I told Vlatko to get up and answer it, but he refused to. But since the telephone went on ringing, I got up, and there was Ivica Kupreskic on the phone. He said, "What are you waiting for? Why don't you go to the shelter? Everybody else has gone." He wanted to speak to Vlatko, and Vlatko came to the telephone. Then they talked, and as they were talking, I woke up the children and Vlatko's parents. We hurriedly got ready and set off to the shelter. When we came out, I locked the door of the passage and I locked the entrance door. So we hurried to the shelter, passing by Ivica Kupreskic's house. We went down through the woods, reached Niko Sakic's house, and I saw Nika Sakic. He was standing in his yard, saying that we should move on because his house was full. Across Niko Sakic's house I saw Dragan Samija. So we moved on. Some five or six hundred metres down the road, I saw Mr. Milan Samija and his wife, Mara. They were feeding sheep. When we reached the playground, I could already hear shots being fired in Ahmici, and then we hurried to the shelter to save ourselves. When we reached the shelter, I found in front of it Anto Kupreskic, Marko Santic, Alojzije Vidovic and Ivo Vidovic. When we entered the shelter, the shelter was full of children, women, elderly persons, men.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: We did not hear quite well. Which members of the household went to the shelter?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Well, it was Vlatko, myself, our children, Vlatko's mother. But Vlatko's father stayed behind in the house because he was ill. He had a surgical intervention on his hip, and he needed to use sticks to walk, so he couldn't move and he stayed behind. So everybody else left, except that Vlatko Kupreskic's father stayed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: So will you please tell us what time was it when you left the house, as far as you can remember?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: I believe it could have been somewhere around half past 5.00 and 6.00. It is difficult to be accurate, but it could have been about that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: But roughly speaking, it was before the firing began?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: We left before the fire began, but we had reached the playgrounds, and I remember it perfectly. I could show it immediately, when I heard the first shots in Ahmici. I could really show that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Some witnesses affirm that that morning, around half past 6.00, that they saw Vlatko wearing a blue coat, passing by the house of Suhrija Ahmic. Could you comment on this and tell us if that is true?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: That is not true, because Vlatko was with me all the time, and I am dead certain about that. And besides, it was so cold for two days before that -- it rained for two days before that, so I mean -- but my husband has never had a blue, light coat, and that is true. That I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Right. Now we've got to the shelter. Please, did Vlatko stay with you in the shelter?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Vlatko stayed there in the shelter until about 10.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: What did he do at 10.00, where did he go?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Around 10.00, Vlatko left the shelter, went to see his father, because the fire had somewhat abated and we were all worried about Vlatko's father.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: So it was around 10.00?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: When did he come back?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: He returned sometime in the afternoon. It could have been around 4.00. I know it was lunchtime. I know we were all hungry.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: When he came back, what did he tell you, where had he been and what had he seen?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: He told me he had been home, that he had seen his father frightened, that the house was full of soldiers, that fire was open from the house, that our house had been looted, that the entrance door had been broken down.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Tell me, after he returned to the shelter, did he go out again, did he leave the shelter again?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Since he could not bring his dad because the fires had started again, sometime as the sun was setting or after sunset, he went back to see his father around 8.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Then he returned to the shelter?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: He returned to the shelter.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: How long did you stay in that shelter?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: In that shelter, we stayed until the next day, that is, until the 17th of April, it was Saturday, until the evening hours, around 8.00, we all left the shelter because all the houses around were aflame, so we left the shelter. In a column, we panicked and set out for Donja Rovna.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: And was Vlatko with you all the time and did he also set off to Donja Rovna?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Vlatko was with us all the time, and he went with us to Donja Rovna.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: So after that period of time of the 16th of April, could you tell us what did Vlatko do or, rather, where was he?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: We spent a fortnight or so in Donja Rovna. There were very many of us. We were sleeping on the floor, and since there were no living conditions, then we moved to Vitez. But Vlatko was there all the time. However, he did go to Vitez now and then because we had absolutely no food supplies there in Donja Rovna, and Vlatko would go and bring us some foodstuffs.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: And where was Vlatko's father, Franjo, during that time?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Vlatko's father, Franjo, was with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Did Franjo Kupreskic, Vlatko's father, tell you what had happened on the day, on the 16th of April, in your house while he was in it?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Yes, he did tell me about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Could you recount briefly what he told you?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: He said that when we left, he stayed behind, he locked the door, and went back to bed. So he went back to bed, and then he heard the fire, and he got up and went to the bathroom. As he stood in the bathroom, he heard a knocking, banging, on the first floor of the house. He didn't know what was going on, but the fire had already been opened. As he was in the bathroom, there was a powerful bang, so that panes burst, and he came out of the bathroom and was standing in the passage and was thinking what to do, whether to stay in the house or go out. He was afraid. But then he went out of the house and he saw three camouflaged soldiers, and they told him, "Hands up." They asked him, "Who might you be?" and he said, "I'm Franjo." "Which Franjo," he said. "Do you have any identity documents?" He said, "Yes, I do, but they are in my coat in the passage, my identity card." "Show it to us." So he showed it to them, and they left him alone. He asked, "What's going on?" and they told him, "Don't ask." Then he went back to the ground floor, where he stayed for a while, and when the fire seemed to calm down, he went to the first floor to see what was going on there. There he saw that the door had been broken out and there was a beam which had fallen down, and the soil from flower pots was all around. They were looking for money. They asked him, "Where is the money?" He told them, "As far as I know, all the money we had we invested in the building of the warehouse," because that was what we were building in Pirici, that warehouse. "I don't know. There is no money." "Oh, come on. Such a well-appointed house and yet no money?" "I know nothing about that. I don't know where the money is." So he saw them take out all the clothes from the wardrobe, and he also saw them, as they climbed to the loft, that they took the synthesiser which belonged to my son Igor. He asked them to leave it behind, but of course he had no say in the matter. That is how it was. I remember that he also told me, as he was standing in front of the house, how our neighbour Cazim Ahmici was passing by, and he asked him to give him an axe. "I dared not give him the axe [realtime error corrected]. I could not decide about that. I had to ask those uniformed men if I could do it. So I went to the shed, I took the axe, and I went back to the house, took a blanket, and I gave them to my neighbour Cazim to help him."

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Excuse me. I just read in the transcript -- something is wrong in the transcript, so it is not quite clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: What did Franjo Kupreskic give Cazim Ahmic? What did the former ask him or what did he give him?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Cazim Ahmic asked Vlatko's father to help him. He asked for an axe and for a blanket. He wanted to make something. I don't know, some makeshift stretcher or something of the sort.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Could you make a correction in the transcript? It's not "eggs," it's "axe."

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: "Axe," a-x-e.

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: An axe to make a kind of a stretcher for his wife, who had been wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: For his wounded wife, he asked for an axe, and then he had to ask for the permission from the soldiers. Have we clarified this? So to make a stretcher for his wounded wife?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: He asked for the permission from the soldiers?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: He asked them if he -- "May I give it to him," because of course he could not do it on his own, and they said they could do it but that she was done and over with.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Do you remember anything else? What did Franjo Kupreskic tell you, something else too, or was that more or less it?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: (No audible response)

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness did not say anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Is Franjo Kupreskic alive?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Vlatko's father died in September '95.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Will you now please answer a series of some different questions? First, could you please tell us, on what kind of terms were you with the Pezer family before the 16th of April, '93?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: We were on good terms. That is, there was mutual respect. We looked after one another, we helped one another. There was never any trouble.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Could you tell us, who is Nevzudin Pezer?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Nevzudin Pezer, Pedja, is Ismail Pezer's son, and his mother was Fata.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: After the 16th of April, '93, did you see Nevzudin Pezer, the son of Ismail and Fata Pezer?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did see him after the 16th of April, '94. I did see Nevzudin Pezer.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Will you please describe that meeting briefly? That is, tell us where it was, when, who was present at the time, and the kind of conversation that you heard.

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: It was in a warehouse in our shop in Pirici. As far as I can remember, it was sometime in late 1994. Nevzudin Pezer turned up one morning in a van driven by Amir Jusic, and Mirhad Salibasic, called Djule, was also with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Will you tell us, these two individuals whom you mentioned, are they Croats or Muslims?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: These two persons are Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Yes. Go on, please.

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: In the store, Mr. Haris Vehabovic was waiting. He often bought deep-frozen food from us, as he himself was a butcher and had his shop in Zenica, and they often came to us to purchase the foodstuffs. So that in the store there were our worker's brother, not a girl, Vlatko, myself, our children, and these persons who arrived in a van.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: What did you talk about? What kind of a meeting was that? Was it the first time that you saw Nevzudin after the war?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Well, we greeted one another in a friendly way, and Nevzudin put his arm around Vlatko's shoulders as if to hug him. It was a cordial meeting. For the first time after the conflict, after that tragedy with a mat (phoen), we talked about everything. I specifically asked if his people were all right, because there was rumour that they had been killed, that is, his wife and his children. But he told us that they had managed to escape and that they were accommodated somewhere in Cajdras in Zenica. From him, I heard that his sister had been wounded, and I already knew that his mother had been killed, because my neighbour, Stipan, had told me that he had seen Fata Pezer's body. I remembered that story, because he told me that he had been told by somebody, and I don't remember who, that a man had put on women's clothes, Muslim clothes, that is, the pantaloons, and he was curious. He wanted to know who that was. When he got there, he saw that it was Fata Pezer's body.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: During that conversation, was there any mention of how Fata Pezer was killed? Was there any mention of that at all? Did you ask him, "Did you have any losses?"

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Well, he said, "My mother was killed and my sister is wounded."

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Will you tell us, please, if you knew at that time that Vlatko had been accused of participating in the killing of Fata, Nevzudin's mother?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: I could not know that because it's -- I mean something like that would have never occurred to me. I wouldn't think it possible to have Vlatko accused of killing Nevzudin's mother.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: But did Nevzudin Pezer know at that time that Vlatko was being charged with the killing of his mother?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Well, had he known, he wouldn't have come to see us. That is not true. I mean, he couldn't have known. He must have spoken to his relatives, to his friends, about what had happened that morning, because he told us then that he had not been there in the house, that he had been in Mahala, in the old part of Vitez, because he was a military policeman. And that morning, he also turned up in a military uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Could you tell us, on what kind of terms were you with Sakib Ahmic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, may I just add something about Nevzudin because I didn't finish it. So we talked about everything, and when Nevzudin was about to leave, I packed some presents for his children, some sweets, and some cigarettes for him, because they told us they were in very dire straits, that they had no income whatsoever. I also asked if Sabahudin Muratovic's children were alive. I asked him because they used to play with my children, and he told me, "Yes, they were alive," and I also packed some presents for them. That is what I wanted to add about Nevzudin Pezer.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: My next question is: On what terms were you with the family of Sakib Ahmic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: With Sakib Ahmic, and with all our neighbours, Sakib Ahmic and whoever his land bordered on were on bad terms with him, regardless of whether they were Muslims or Croats, but relations with his children were normal and good.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: After the 16th of April, did you see Sakib or his granddaughter Enisa?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: No, I never saw his granddaughter Enisa. As for Sakib, I remember seeing him once in Ahmici in a column of people. There was a visit organised. As for his granddaughter, I don't think I could recognise her. She was a year or two older than my daughter. She probably has changed, so I couldn't recognise her.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, I will be through with one section of this testimony in a couple of minutes, if I may be allowed to overstep the time for a few minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Did you hear that Enisa came to Ahmici to take a video recording of her house?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: No, I hadn't heard about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Did Vlatko tell you that he saw her or that he spoke to her?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: No, Vlatko didn't tell me. Probably if it was true he would have told me. I don't believe it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Could you tell me what your relations were with Rasim Gradinovic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: With Rasim Gradinovic, we were on good terms. He often worked as a manual labourer for us, particularly in 1992, while we were building the warehouse in Pirici.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Could you tell us what his health was like?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Rasim Gradinovic is a sick man. I know that he took a swim in the Lasva River, as a result of which he had a kind of stroke and became psychologically unstable. I know that he worked in a socially-owned enterprise belonging to Travnik municipality. He was a driver of a lorry. But since that stroke, he was on sick leave most of the time, and he was unfit for work. I also know that he married several times, that he liked to have a drink or two. I also remember that when we completed work on the building in Pirici, we prepared a celebration. There was a large percentage of Muslims, and I remember in particular when Ramiz's (sic) wife came to take him home after midnight. He was so drunk that she had to drag him along the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: My left question for today: Do you know Cizmo Senija and her husband?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: No, I've never heard of her.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Mr. President, I should like to end the examination for today. I have some documents to show the witness which I would like to do tomorrow. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll adjourn now until tomorrow at 9.00.
